q: Who is the author of the essay "Sanskriti"?
e: The chapter "Sanskriti" is an essay written by renowned Buddhist scholar and Hindi prose writer Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan.

q: What was the childhood name of Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan?
e: Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan was born in 1905 in Sohana village, Punjab, and his childhood name was Harnamdas.

q: In which year and state was Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan born?
e: He was born in 1905 in Sohana village in the Ambala district of undivided Punjab.

q: Under which literary genre does the chapter "Sanskriti" fall?
e: "Sanskriti" is a reflective and analytical essay that clarifies the distinction between civilization and culture.

q: According to the author, which two words are least understood yet most frequently used?
e: At the start of the essay, the author observes that "sabhyata" (civilization) and "sanskriti" (culture) are the most used yet least understood words.

q: According to the author, what is "civilization" (sabhyata) the result of?
e: According to the author, civilization is the outcome of culture; culture creates, while civilization is its external product.

q: Which two ancient inventions are primarily cited in the chapter to explain culture?
o: Discovery of fire and invention of needle and thread
e: Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan uses the discovery of fire and the invention of needle and thread to illustrate a cultured (sanskrit) person.

q: According to the chapter, what should the person who first conceived fire or tools like needle and wheel be called?
e: The one who possessed the inner creative impulse and capability to invent something new is called a "sanskrit" (cultured) person.

q: People today who merely use fire, wheels, or needle-and-thread discovered by ancestors can be called what?
e: Descendants who effortlessly use their ancestors’ inventions without inventing anew are called "civilized" (sabhya), not necessarily cultured.

q: Which scientist does the author cite as the discoverer of the law of gravitation?
e: The author cites Newton as an example of a "cultured human" because he discovered the principle of gravitation.

q: How does the author describe today’s physics student in comparison to Newton?
o: More civilized than Newton, though not as cultured as Newton
e: Today’s student knows more facts (about atoms, etc.), so they may be called more civilized, but not as cultured (inventive) as Newton.

q: What kind of inspirations behind human culture are "hunger" (pet ki aag) and "clothing the body" considered?
e: Satisfying hunger and protecting the body from heat and cold are physical/material needs that drove many inventions.

q: A person sleeping under the open sky wondering about the stars like a "tray of pearls" is an example of which impulse?
e: This wonder has nothing to do with food or clothing; it represents pure intellectual curiosity, a mother of culture.

q: Which Russian leader’s example did the author give to illustrate the spirit of humanity?
e: The author mentions that Lenin used to give away the dry pieces of bread kept in his desk to hungry others instead of eating them himself.

q: Who spent his entire life in hardship hoping to see the workers of the world happy?
e: The text states that Karl Marx spent his entire life in hardship dreaming of happiness for the workers of the world.

q: Two and a half thousand years ago, who renounced his kingdom and home to see craving-torn humanity happy?
e: Siddhartha (Gautama Buddha) left his palace not due to material lack, but out of compassion for humanity’s suffering.

q: When culture loses its connection with the spirit of human welfare, what does it become?
e: The author explicitly states that once severed from the spirit of welfare, culture turns into "asanskriti" (anti-culture).

q: According to the author, what is the inevitable outcome of "asanskriti" (anti-culture)?
e: Just as culture yields civilization, anti-culture devoid of welfare inevitably yields barbarism (asabhyata).

q: Which two adjectives, according to the author, create further confusion when attached to civilization and culture?
e: The author notes that attaching the adjectives "material" and "spiritual" to civilization and culture makes their meaning even harder to grasp.

q: With which great personality did Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan spend a long time at Wardha?
e: Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan stayed with Mahatma Gandhi in Wardha for a long period and worked for the promotion of Hindi.

q: Of which ancient language and religion was Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan an eminent scholar?
e: He was a Buddhist monk and an eminent scholar of the Pali language and Buddhism; he also translated the Jataka tales.

q: Which of the following works is written by Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan?
e: "Bhikshu ke Patra", "Jo Na Bhool Saka", "Aah! Aisi Daridrata", and "Rail ka Ticket" are his notable works.

q: According to the chapter, what kind of entity is "human culture" (manav sanskriti)?
e: In the concluding section, the author emphasizes that human culture is an indivisible whole that cannot be compartmentalized.

q: A mother holding her sick child in her lap all night is an example of which quality?
e: A mother staying awake all night for her sick child symbolizes selfless human compassion beyond any material gain.

q: What term does the author use for the superstitions and rigid customs carried on in the name of culture?
e: The author remarks that the heap of rubbish people carry in the name of culture is not worthy of preservation.

q: Dry pieces of what item did Lenin keep in his desk to feed others?
e: Lenin kept dry pieces of bread in his desk and gave them to others rather than eating them himself, reflecting his selflessness.

q: Which elements in human culture prove permanent and enduring?
e: The author believes that whatever promotes human welfare endures in human culture, while harmful elements perish.

q: In which year did Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan pass away?
e: Renowned essayist and Buddhist scholar Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan passed away in 1988.

q: What is the innate human tendency that inspires new inventions and human welfare called?
e: According to the essay, that innate inner impulse and capability is "culture", while its external utilization is "civilization".

q: A cultured person discovers something new, yet how do their descendants receive it?
e: The cultured inventor toils to discover something, while descendants inherit and use that achievement effortlessly.

q: How is "civilization" (sabhyata) identified in the chapter?
o: In ways of eating, dressing, travelling, and using invented facilities
By the number of wars fought
e: Civilization is the external lifestyle, habits, and facilities humans inherit as outcomes of cultural inventions.

q: Which invention does the author link to the concern of protecting oneself from cold and heat?
o: Invention of needle, thread, and clothing
e: The need to cover the body and shield against heat and cold inspired humans to pierce metal and invent the needle and thread.

q: If an early human thought of producing fire to roast raw meat, what was their greatest distinction in the author’s view?
o: They possessed the creative insight and capability (sanskriti) to invent
They were king of the jungle
e: Conceiving and producing fire instead of eating raw food proved that early human’s "cultured" (sanskrit) creative power.

q: How can early humans’ "invention of the wheel" be viewed in terms of culture and civilization?
o: Conceiving the wheel is culture, while using it in modern vehicles is civilization
The wheel is merely a toy
Using the wheel is culture and conceiving it is civilization
e: By the essay’s framework, the original creative insight behind the wheel (like fire or needle) is culture, and society’s ongoing use of it is civilization.

q: To what does the author refer with the poetic phrase "tray filled with pearls" (motiyon bhara thaal)?
e: A person sleeping under the open sky gazes at the stars wondering what this "tray of pearls" is—an example of pure curiosity.

q: What is the correct meaning of the word "anaayas" used in the chapter?
e: "Anaayas" means effortlessly; descendants receive their ancestors’ discoveries without having to reinvent them.

q: What does the compound word "sheet-ushna" used in the text signify?
e: "Sheet-ushna" means cold and heat, protection against which spurred inventions like stitched clothing.

q: What does the author call the intellect or capability that invents weapons of self-destruction?
e: When intellect invents tools of mass destruction against human welfare, it is not culture but anti-culture (asanskriti).

q: How do the "great souls" (mahamanav) mentioned in the chapter live their lives?
o: Caring only for their own family
Sacrificing personal comfort for the welfare of others
e: Great souls like Buddha, Karl Marx, and Lenin sacrificed personal comfort to relieve the suffering of fellow humans.

q: What is the correct meaning of the word "avibhajya"?
o: That which cannot be divided or fragmented
e: "Avibhajya" means indivisible; according to the author, the welfare-oriented culture of humanity is one indivisible whole.

q: Which quality does the author note is NOT guaranteed simply by being "civilized" (sabhya)?
o: Possessing original inventive capability (sanskriti) or humane compassion
e: Someone enjoying modern conveniences appears civilized, yet may lack original creative culture or moral compassion.

q: What does the author imply by asking whether only an "idle" (nithalla) person gazes at the stars?
o: He rises above mere bodily survival to pursue pure intellectual curiosity
He likes sleeping during the day
e: Utilitarians who reduce everything to survival might call a stargazer idle, yet such curiosity actually births science and philosophy.

q: According to the author, is it proper to divide culture into narrow compartments?
o: No, because welfare-oriented human culture is an indivisible whole
The author expresses no view on this
e: The author firmly holds that human culture is indivisible and splitting its welfare-oriented essence along sectarian lines is wrong.

q: How is the word "Bhikshu" connected to Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan’s own life?
o: He only acted as a beggar
He took Buddhist ordination and lived as a Buddhist monk (bhikshu)
e: Harnamdas embraced Buddhism, became a Buddhist monk (bhikshu), and became known as Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan.

q: In which context is the word "trishna" (craving/greed) used in the chapter?
o: Siddhartha (Buddha) renouncing his palace on seeing humanity fighting under the grip of craving
e: Seeing humanity torn apart by endless craving (trishna), Siddhartha renounced his throne to seek a path of peace.

q: In what context is the word "sarvanash" (total destruction) used in the essay?
o: Anti-culture inventing weapons and means that destroy humanity
e: When human inventiveness abandons welfare to create destructive weapons, it drives humanity toward total ruin (barbarism).

q: Which claim is the example of the "mother" used to refute in the essay?
o: That every human action is driven solely by material self-interest of food and clothing
e: If only material self-interest drove humans, a mother would never stay awake selflessly all night for her sick child.

q: Whom does the author call a "truly cultured person" (asli sanskrit vyakti)?
o: One who discovers a new truth through intellect or sacrifices for human welfare
e: Creative power to discover new truths and selfless devotion to human welfare define a truly cultured person.

q: What subtle intelligence is revealed in the "invention of needle and thread"?
o: Grinding a piece of metal, piercing an eye at one end, and threading it to join two pieces of cloth
e: The author vividly describes how shaping a metal splinter, piercing an eye, and threading it to stitch cloth was a remarkable creative leap.

q: Why does the author treat the "spirit of welfare" (kalyan ki bhavna) as the touchstone of culture?
o: Because without it, even an intelligent inventor can become destructive
e: Knowledge and inventions without moral welfare become destructive; hence humanity and welfare are the true test of culture.

q: What is the meaning of the word "rakshaniya" used in "Sanskriti"?
e: "Rakshaniya" means worthy of preservation; the author argues that superstitions heaped in culture’s name are not worth preserving.

q: What is the main difference between the original discoverer of fire and someone cooking on a gas stove today?
o: The first was cultured (an inventor), whereas today’s user is merely civilized through that inheritance
e: The inventor imagined fire from scratch and was cultured, while the modern user of convenient stoves is simply civilized.

q: According to the author, what part of supposed "culture" should be discarded over time?
o: Harmful customs, superstitions, and the heap of rubbish
e: For human progress, outdated, harmful customs—described as rubbish—must be shed rather than blindly preserved.

q: Which philosophical influence is clearly visible in the author’s ideas in "Sanskriti"?
o: Buddhist compassion, Gandhian ethics, and humanist thought
e: Citing Buddha, Lenin, and Marx alongside emphasis on welfare and indivisible humanity reflects Buddhist compassion and humanism.

q: If a society has skyscrapers and fast vehicles yet lacks moral sensitivity and compassion, how would the author view it?
o: Outwardly civilized in conveniences, yet devoid of true culture
e: Material gadgets give only external civilization; true culture requires moral welfare, humanity, and creativity.

q: What is the chief characteristic of Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan’s prose style?
o: Simple, logical, conversational, and analytical prose enriched with concrete examples
e: The author clarifies a complex philosophical topic using everyday examples (fire, needle, mother, Newton) and direct reasoning.

q: In what context is the word "jwala" (fire/flame) used in the essay?
o: To describe the fire of hunger ("pet ki jwala") when explaining motives behind inventions
e: The author asks whether culture arises solely from the "flame of the belly" (hunger) and physical survival needs.

q: When humans mechanically use existing tools without thinking of anything new, what are they demonstrating?
o: Merely consuming the products of civilization
e: Passively using ready-made ancestral inventions is merely enjoying civilization, whereas new creative or benevolent thought is culture.

q: To what does the word "akalyankari" (harmful/non-beneficial) refer in the text?
o: Elements and inventions that cause harm and destruction
e: Whatever opposes human welfare and breeds destruction is "akalyankari", and cannot endure under the name of culture.

q: Which quality does the author place highest in the name of humanity?
o: Altruism, compassion, sacrifice, and selfless welfare
e: Compassion, sacrifice, and public welfare are upheld by the author as the highest expression of human culture.

q: A person uses modern smartphones and airplanes yet feels envy and creates nothing new. According to the essay, how should they be classified?
o: Civilized (a consumer of conveniences), though not truly cultured
e: Using modern gadgets merely shows external civilization; without creative spirit or benevolent character, one is not truly cultured.

q: If a scientist invents a deadly chemical weapon capable of killing millions, what would Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan call this invention?
e: Intellect severed from human welfare that invents tools of mass slaughter is explicitly termed "anti-culture" leading to barbarism.

q: A student in class recites Newton’s laws and modern quantum theory, yet why does the author not regard the student as equally "cultured" as Newton?
o: Because the student does not know English
Because the student merely inherits and recites existing knowledge (civilized), while Newton originally discovered it
e: Inheriting discovered knowledge makes one civilized, whereas the original creative power to uncover an unknown truth is culture.

q: Even when not hungry, if an astronomer studies planetary motion all night through a telescope, which idea from the essay does this confirm?
o: Beyond physical needs, pure thirst for knowledge is also a major source of culture
e: Like the stargazer wondering at the "tray of pearls", selfless curiosity beyond survival needs also generates culture.

q: If some people defend harmful caste prejudices or superstitions as "our culture", what response does this chapter provide?
o: Superstitions opposing human welfare are not culture but "rubbish" that must be discarded
e: The author clarifies that deadwood and rubbish piled up in the name of culture are not worth saving; only welfare-promoting values endure.

q: Lenin giving away his dry bread and Siddhartha renouncing his palace—what common thread links both examples?
o: Both rose above self-interest out of deep compassion to relieve others’ suffering
e: Despite different eras and places, the exact same benevolent human culture inspired both of them.

q: "A cultured person discovers something new, but their descendant receives it effortlessly from the ancestor." — Which option best illustrates this?
o: A doctor’s son becoming a doctor without study
A child built a brand new toy
An ancestor invented the wheel or fire, and today’s generation effortlessly uses vehicles and stoves
A farmer sowed a new crop
e: Original inventions by ancestors pass effortlessly to future generations, becoming part of everyday civilization.

q: When someone first tied logs together to make a raft to cross a river, how would the essay classify that person’s act?
o: Manifestation of culture (original insight and creative capability)
e: The original insight solving a human challenge is "culture", whereas routine boat travel afterward becomes "civilization".

q: Why does the author call civilization the outcome of culture, rather than culture the outcome of civilization?
o: Because creative thought/impulse (culture) must arise first within humans before external tools and lifestyles (civilization) emerge
Because nobody can think without clothes
Because culture exists only in books
e: Just as a tree cannot grow without a seed, external civilization cannot exist without the inner creative seed of culture.

q: Though poor, a person shares half his bread with a hungry traveller. In the author’s eyes, what kind of person is he?
o: A deeply cultured human being, due to his spirit of sacrifice and compassion
e: As Lenin’s example shows, sharing with others even amid scarcity reflects true inner culture and humanity.

q: If two nations claim separate, superior cultures and wage war over it, what illusion are they under according to the essay’s conclusion?
o: They fail to see that true welfare-oriented human culture is indivisible, and waging war is anti-culture
They should speak only their own language
e: The essay concludes that true human culture is indivisible and benevolent; spreading hatred and war is anti-culture.

q: When people debate civilization and culture by adding adjectives like "material" and "spiritual", what does the author suggest?
o: Instead of getting tangled in heavy jargon, we should understand their core difference through concrete examples
We should stop using the word culture
e: Setting aside confusing labels, the author clarifies the terms clearly through concrete examples like fire, needle, Newton, and Buddha.

q: Why did the author include the example of Karl Marx even though he himself was a Buddhist monk?
o: To show that the culture of human welfare belongs to no single religion or sect, but is universal
To belittle Marx compared to Buddha
e: By placing Buddha, Karl Marx, and Lenin together, the author himself demonstrates that humane culture transcends sectarian borders.

q: A person lives in a lavish house and wears expensive clothes, yet disrespects his aged parents. According to the chapter, what does he lack?
o: True human culture (welfare and moral sensitivity)
e: Outward luxury may give an appearance of civilization, yet without moral sensitivity and compassion one lacks true culture.

q: Why has the author accorded such high honour to ordinary inventions like "fire" and "needle and thread"?
o: Because they are still expensive today
Because he had no bigger examples
Because conceiving them from scratch in that primitive era was a revolutionary leap of human intellect
Because they were made only in India
e: In an age with no prior technology, inventing fire or the needle from nothing was as monumental as any modern breakthrough.

q: If an old tradition spreads discrimination and suffering in society, what should our duty be according to the author?
o: Consider it the best part of culture
Treat it as "rubbish", discard it, and embrace welfare-promoting values
e: Whatever harms human welfare cannot be true culture; society progresses only by discarding harmful deadwood.

q: "Are hunger and covering the body the sole mothers of culture?" — In what direction does the author answer this question?
o: No; alongside material needs, disinterested curiosity and the spirit of human welfare are also mothers of culture
Yes, there is no other motive
e: Through the stargazer, the mother, Siddhartha, Marx, and Lenin, the author proves selfless curiosity and compassion equally generate culture.

q: How does the chapter’s use of "sanskrit" (cultured) differ from its casual everyday meaning (merely polite/well-dressed)?
o: In the chapter it means only dressing well
In the chapter it signifies creative inventiveness, pursuit of truth, and selfless compassion
In the chapter it means speaking Sanskrit
e: Commonly equated with polite manners, Kausalyayan defines true culture as creative discovery and selfless human welfare.

q: If a student concludes from "Sanskriti" that "we should simply boast about ancestors’ inventions and do nothing new", which idea of the text does this violate?
o: We should smash all old tools
Passive consumption leaves us merely civilized; without new inquiry and compassionate creation, we cannot be cultured
e: The essay teaches that merely enjoying ancestral feats is civilization; we become cultured through fresh inquiry and welfare-driven action.

q: "Whatever promotes human welfare never perishes and becomes woven into human culture." — Which example confirms this?
o: The enduring legacy of fire, the wheel, the needle, and the compassion of Buddha and great humanists
e: Welfare-enhancing inventions and moral ideals survive millennia as the shared heritage of all humanity.

q: Why does the author repeatedly use rhetorical questions ("Who should be called cultured?", etc.) in the essay?
o: To spark curiosity and actively engage the reader in critical reflection
Because the author did not know the answers
e: This conversational questioning style prevents blind acceptance and guides the reader through logical reflection.

q: If a nation builds nuclear bombs while its citizens starve, how would Kausalyayan classify that achievement?
e: Devoid of welfare, creating destructive weapons is anti-culture driving humanity toward ruin rather than civilization.

q: In the context of the essay, what relationship is established between "welfare/ethics" and "science"?
o: Scientific discovery becomes true culture only when guided by human welfare and ethics
e: The author is not anti-science (he praises Newton), but insists that scientific intellect must stay anchored in human welfare.

q: The relationship between "culture" and "civilization" resembles which pair?
o: Root/inner creative impulse and its outward fruit/result
e: Culture is the creative and humane root within, while civilization is the outward fruit or outcome borne by it.

q: When a doctor selflessly risks his life to treat patients during an epidemic without greed, what does this exemplify?
o: True culture rooted in human welfare and compassion
e: Risking personal comfort to save others directly embodies the selfless welfare spirit defined as true culture in the essay.

q: By recognizing "curiosity" (kautuhal) as a source of culture, which human faculty does the author honour?
o: The free intellectual and imaginative capacity to seek truth
e: Curiosity to explore nature and the cosmos sets humans apart and drives cultural and scientific discovery.

q: What attitude toward our ancestors’ legacy does the chapter "Sanskriti" inspire?
o: Blindly obey everything from the past
Remain grateful for their beneficial discoveries while shedding harmful superstitions and creating anew
e: We should cherish beneficial achievements from the past while discarding harmful customs and continuing creative progress.

q: What connects the "mother holding her sick child" and the "early human discovering fire" in the essay?
o: One solved a survival challenge and the other acted out of selfless love—both reveal dimensions of human culture
e: Together these examples show that culture lives not only in intellectual inventions, but equally in the compassion of the heart.

q: "Should we call the capability that invents tools of self-destruction culture or anti-culture?" — What does the author establish with this question?
o: Without the spirit of welfare, no invention deserves to be called culture
e: The author establishes an ethical standard: creativity is judged by whether it serves human welfare rather than destruction.

q: According to "Sanskriti", how should any nation’s true progress be measured?
o: By its citizens’ welfare-driven consciousness, humanity, and creative culture
By the number of old superstitions
e: Rather than outward show, human welfare, compassion, and truth-seeking measure a society’s genuine cultural height.

Reason (R): Culture is the inner capability and impulse that drives new discovery, whereas civilization is the outward result of that discovery.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is true, but R is false because the early inventor had no formal university degree; innate creative insight made him cultured.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because disinterested curiosity and compassion also generate culture beyond survival needs; R is true.

Reason (R): Such anti-culture results not in civilization, but in barbarism (asabhyata) that creates tools of human destruction.

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains the destructive outcome of anti-culture divorced from human welfare.

Reason (R): He set out in search of a path of human welfare to relieve humanity fighting under the grip of craving.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because Siddhartha lacked no material comfort in the palace; he left out of compassion. R is true.

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains why the author cited Lenin’s gesture.

Reason (R): Practices that go against human welfare are merely a heap of rubbish and are not worth preserving.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because the author argues against preserving superstitions; R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan believes that human culture is an indivisible whole.
Reason (R): Welfare-oriented truths, compassion, and beneficial discoveries belong to all humanity rather than being confined to one caste, religion, or nation.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains why human culture is indivisible.

Reason (R): In this essay, the author uses concrete everyday examples to clarify the fundamental difference between the two terms.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: A is false because the author states at the outset that adding "material" and "spiritual" creates greater confusion; R is true.

q:

Reason (R): Like any cultured person, he was seeking only his own personal luxury.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

q: What is the central philosophical message of the essay "Sanskriti"?
o: Creative truth-seeking and selfless human welfare constitute true culture, without which even science breeds barbarism
Humans should gather only material wealth
All ancient customs must be followed blindly
e: The essay’s core thesis is that without ethics, compassion, and welfare-driven creativity, material or scientific progress cannot become true culture.

q: How is Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan’s essay relevant in the age of modern AI and digital technology?
o: It warns that if technology serves destruction or exploitation instead of human welfare, it becomes anti-culture and barbarism
It tells us to only farm
It narrates the history of the internet
e: Technology is a tool: guided by human welfare it enriches civilization, whereas divorced from ethics it turns into anti-culture.

q: Why did the author compare "Newton" and a "modern student" to clarify the contrast between culture and civilization?
o: To show that accumulating inherited information (civilization) and original creative insight (culture) are two distinct levels
To point out Newton’s math errors
e: Learning pre-discovered textbook facts is easy, whereas discovering a fundamental law from scratch requires higher cultural creativity.

q: By declaring "human culture is indivisible", which grave historical problem does the author critique?
o: Religious, racial, and national divisions and supremacist pride carried out in the name of culture
e: Challenging those who fight over sectarian "cultures", the author reminds humanity that every benevolent achievement belongs to all.

q: Comparing humanistic traditions in Hindi literature with Kausalyayan’s principle of "welfare" (kalyan), what common ground emerges?
o: They reject hollow orthodoxy and uphold love, compassion, and public welfare as true religion/culture
e: Rejecting superstitious deadwood while placing compassion and public welfare supreme is shared across India’s humanist tradition.

q: What warning does the concept of "asanskriti" (anti-culture) in the essay convey?
o: That people should stop using fire
That if intellect and science sever ties with ethics, humanity can engineer its own destruction
e: Building tools of self-destruction warns us that technical brilliance without moral conscience is humanity’s gravest peril.

q: What role does "innate human nature" play in creating culture, as clarified by the author?
o: Curiosity, creativity, and compassion are innate human impulses that lay the foundation of civilization
Innate nature has nothing to do with culture
e: Unlike mere survival instincts, human curiosity, imagination, and empathy naturally give rise to culture.

q: "Only that which promotes welfare endures"—By this criterion, which tradition from the past proves to be "rubbish" (kooda-karkat)?
o: Untouchability, superstition, and narrow prejudices degrading fellow humans
e: Practices that breed injustice and suffering are harmful; clinging to them as "culture" blocks human progress.

q: How does the author resolve the dualism between "material" and "spiritual" in the essay "Sanskriti"?
o: By treating them as irreconcilable opposites
By showing that both material needs and spiritual curiosity/compassion unite in creating one humane culture when guided by welfare
By calling the material world an illusion
e: By valuing both fire/needle (material needs) and Buddha/mother (selfless love), the author reconciles material and spiritual creativity.

q: JAC Board exams often ask "What is the main difference between sabhyata and sanskriti?"—Which concise formula answers this best?
o: Culture is old and civilization is new
Culture is inner creative power and welfare consciousness, while civilization is its external usable outcome
Culture is rural and civilization is urban
Civilization is language and culture is geography
e: This core formula—inner creative/humane capacity equals culture, and its outward usable result equals civilization—captures the entire essay.

q: If scientific inventions multiply rapidly in a society while moral values collapse, what outcome does the essay predict?
o: "Anti-culture" and "barbarism" will emerge from within those very tools of civilization
e: Without morality and welfare, technological power turns into an instrument of ruin, which the author calls barbarism.

q: What important lesson does the comparison between the student knowing "atoms and nuclei" and "Newton" offer to our education system?
o: Exams should ask only about Newton
Education must aim not merely at memorizing accumulated facts, but at nurturing curiosity and original thinking
e: Rote memorization only adds surface information; true education awakens inquiry, critical thought, and creative culture.

q: According to Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan, what risk remains even inside a supposedly "highly civilized" society?
o: If it loses the spirit of welfare, that society can plunge into terrible barbarism and self-destruction
e: World wars proved that nations boasting advanced technical civilization can descend into horrific barbarism once compassion is lost.

q: How did placing Siddhartha and Karl Marx after fire and needle-and-thread complete the author’s definition of culture?
o: Merely by lengthening a historical list
By uniting material inventiveness with social justice and spiritual compassion
e: Material invention, intellectual discovery, and moral compassion together form the author’s complete definition of culture.

q: If one wants to explain that "culture is a flowing river, not stagnant ice", which argument from this essay fits best?
o: Accumulated deadwood (superstitions) must be discarded so that only welfare-oriented and creative elements flow forward
e: Rigid superstitions stagnate; living culture continually renews itself by shedding deadwood and embracing beneficial creativity.

q: "A great soul lives for the happiness of all rather than personal comfort"—To which figures in the chapter does this apply 100%?
o: Siddhartha (Gautama Buddha), Karl Marx, and Lenin
e: Across different historical contexts, all three sacrificed personal comfort to alleviate human suffering.

q: What kind of critical thinking does studying "Sanskriti" foster among Class 10 students?
o: The ability to test traditions on the touchstone of "human welfare" rather than accepting them blindly
e: The essay trains students to apply ethical reasoning—testing any custom or technology against human welfare.

q: Which element is completely absent from Bhadant Anand Kausalyayan’s definition of true culture?
o: Narrow sectarianism, violence, and selfish exploitation
e: Sectarianism, violence, and exploitation oppose humanity, so the author classifies them as anti-culture rather than culture.

q: When we speak of "Indus Valley Civilization" or "Modern Civilization", what is primarily being described per Kausalyayan’s framework?
o: Their cities, tools, clothing, transport, and external material achievements and lifestyles
e: Town planning, tools, clothing, and living standards are the outward products of inventiveness that define a civilization.

q: Why did the author use the word "self-destruction" (aatma-vinash) rather than merely "destruction of others"?
o: Because he did not care about others
Because weapons of mass destruction ultimately endanger all humanity, including the inventors themselves
e: Since humanity is one indivisible whole, destroying any part of it with lethal inventions ultimately constitutes self-destruction.

q: How would the author’s framework classify "sparks from striking stones (fire discovery)" versus "detonating an atomic bomb"?
o: The first is welfare-oriented "culture", whereas the second is destructive "anti-culture"
The first is barbarism and the second is culture
e: Both used intellect, yet fire nurtured life and welfare (culture), whereas atomic weapons bring mass ruin (anti-culture).

q: Based on the conclusion of "Sanskriti", which two qualities must coexist in an ideal global citizen?
o: Creative curiosity for truth and compassion for indivisible human welfare
e: Combining creative inquiry with compassionate concern for all humanity makes someone a true cultured global citizen.

q: According to the essay, on what basis are cultural elements divided into "perishable" (nashwar) and "eternal" (shashwat)?
o: Harmful elements perish, while elements serving human welfare endure permanently
Based on foreign or native origin
e: Values that serve humanity survive across ages, while harmful customs and destructive practices fade away.

q: "It is unwise to carry harmful or useless baggage on our heads calling it culture"—Which part of the essay matches this idea?
o: The statement that the "heap of rubbish" carried in the name of culture is not worth preserving
e: The author boldly asserts that superstitious deadwood is not culture and need not be preserved.

q: How did Kausalyayan bring the abstract debate on "culture" and "civilization" within reach of ordinary readers?
o: By offering vivid, relatable examples like fire, needle, a mother, stars, Newton, and Lenin
e: Translating abstract philosophy into vivid everyday examples makes the essay deeply engaging and lucid.

q: If a society uses wheels and electricity yet contributes nothing new to science, art, or human welfare for a century, what is its state?
o: It actively consumes existing "civilization", yet its creative generation of new "culture" has stalled
It returned to the Stone Age
e: Living solely off past achievements is passive consumption of civilization; vibrant culture demands ongoing creativity.

q: Based on the chapter, what best describes the relationship between "morality" (naitikta) and "culture"?
o: Morality and welfare consciousness are the soul of culture; without them culture turns into anti-culture
Morality is only for the weak
e: The author clarifies that mental capability becomes true culture only when anchored in morality and welfare.

q: What thematic bridge connects "Sanskriti" and "Naubaatkhane mein Ibaadat" in the Class 10 Kshitij prose section?
o: Both chapters rise above narrow religious divisions to champion human unity, devotion, and welfare-oriented culture
e: Bismillah Khan lives out an indivisible shared culture, while "Sanskriti" articulates the philosophical foundation of that indivisible human culture.

q: When writing the conclusion for a JAC Board value-based answer on "Sanskriti", which point must be included?
o: Culture is human creative and welfare-driven spirit, civilization is its result, and inventions lacking welfare are anti-culture
Civilization is always greater than culture
e: Summarizing the culture-civilization distinction, the welfare touchstone, and culture’s indivisibility makes an exam answer complete.

q: "What should we call the capability that makes humans invent tools of self-destruction?" — To what conclusion does this question lead the reader?
o: That the "spirit of welfare" guiding invention—not mere cleverness—is true culture
That ancient times had no inventions
That making weapons is also an art
e: Mere cleverness can engineer destruction; true culture channels intellect toward human welfare, peace, and life.
